analysis.one_liner: Imposes a carbon tax on coal, oil, and natural gas, starting at $10 per ton and rising annually until emissions fall sharply.
analysis.headline: A carbon tax on coal, oil, and natural gas starting at $10 per ton was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in January 2009 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Save Our Climate Act would have taxed the carbon content of coal, oil, and natural gas at $10 per ton, with the rate going up $10 every year until U.S. carbon emissions fell to 20% of their 1990 level. The money could have been used to cut taxes for low- and middle-income families or fund clean energy. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill would have reduced the carbon emissions driving climate change, which falls hardest on ordinary communities through extreme weather and rising sea levels. Low- and middle-income households stood to benefit directly if the revenue was used to cut their taxes or fund domestic programs, as the bill contemplated. Renewable energy industries would have gained a cost advantage as fossil fuels became pricier.

how_it_helps.text: By making fossil fuels more expensive in proportion to their carbon content, the tax would push utilities, refineries, and consumers toward cleaner fuels and efficiency, cutting the pollution driving climate change.

The bill's stated intent was that the revenue could be used to cut taxes for low- and middle-income taxpayers or fund clean-energy research and other domestic priorities, cushioning households from the higher energy prices.

Refunds were built in for exported fuels and for fuels whose carbon is embedded or sequestered in manufacturing, so energy-intensive domestic producers would not pay twice on carbon that never entered the atmosphere.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers would have paid the tax upfront and passed it to consumers through higher prices for gasoline, heating oil, natural gas, and electricity. Because low-income households spend a larger share of their income on energy, the tax's burden would have been regressive unless offset by the tax cuts or rebates the bill envisioned but did not require.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers, then energy consumers

drawbacks.text: A carbon tax raises the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, and because low- and middle-income households spend a larger share of their income on energy, the burden falls hardest on them; the bill found that revenue could be used to cut taxes for those households or fund alternatives, but it did not itself mandate any such rebate or offset.

The tax starts at $10 per ton and rises by $10 each year until emissions fall to 20% of 1990 levels—a target that could imply very high fuel prices over decades—with no pause or review mechanism other than a Treasury study every five years, so it committed the economy to escalating energy costs before cleaner alternatives were fully in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside was a steadily escalating price on carbon—the tool most economists consider the simplest way to cut emissions—with refundable credits that protected energy-intensive manufacturers and exporters, and the cost (higher energy prices) was real and regressive but, as the bill's own findings noted, could have been offset with low- and middle-income tax relief or green energy funding. The main design weaknesses: the bill left the use of revenue unspecified rather than guaranteeing households would be made whole, and it never advanced far enough to be amended or debated. Its biggest cost, ultimately, was that it never got a hearing at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Pete Stark introduced the Save Our Climate Act on January 15, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee, which he chaired.
The complete action history shows nothing after the referral: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action for the rest of the 111th Congress.

The bill would have imposed a $10-per-ton tax on the carbon content of coal, petroleum, and natural gas, with the rate increasing by $10 every year until U.S. emissions fell to 20% of their 1990 level.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and consumers of coal, oil, and gas are better off because the tax never happened; anyone hoping for federal climate pricing in that Congress gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three cosponsors were all Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; no vote ever occurred, so partisan lines were never formally tested.

industries.note: Coal has the highest carbon content per unit of energy of any fossil fuel, so a per-ton carbon tax raises its cost more than oil or gas, accelerating the shift away from coal-fired power. Miners and coal communities bear the adjustment costs.

The tax applies at the point of first sale by the manufacturer, producer, or importer, so refiners and importers of petroleum products and natural gas pay it upfront and pass the cost through to consumers at the pump and on heating bills.
By raising the price of carbon-based fuels, the tax makes wind, solar, and efficiency relatively more competitive without requiring direct subsidies.
